blocks.html_en: We study the scaling behavior of byte Transformers, and the main findings are: 1) with two modeling ingredients (token-superposition training (Peng et al., 2026) and hash embeddings), byte Transformers consistently outperform subword Transformers when scaling the number of parameters (Figure 1a). 2) Byte models remain effective as training data continues to scale. Given a fixed FLOPs budget (Figure 1c), the optimal proportion between data and parameters is around 1.5 to 3 times that of subword models. These results motivate a different perspective on sequence length: rather than treating longer sequences as a defect, they can provide additional computation under the same parameter budget, which is a useful scaling axis for language models. Further evaluations on downstream text-only and vision–language tasks show that byte Transformers significantly improve performance on tasks that require fine-grained perception (around 40%40\% relative improvements over subword Transformers on CUTE scores, 20%20\% on OCRBench (Liu et al., 2024)).

sentences.en: We study the scaling behavior of byte Transformers, and the main findings are: 1) with two modeling ingredients (token-superposition training (Peng et al., 2026) and hash embeddings), byte Transformers consistently outperform subword Transformers when scaling the number of parameters (Figure 1a).
2) Byte models remain effective as training data continues to scale.
Given a fixed FLOPs budget (Figure 1c), the optimal proportion between data and parameters is around 1.5 to 3 times that of subword models.

These results motivate a different perspective on sequence length: rather than treating longer sequences as a defect, they can provide additional computation under the same parameter budget, which is a useful scaling axis for language models.

Further evaluations on downstream text-only and vision–language tasks show that byte Transformers significantly improve performance on tasks that require fine-grained perception (around 40%40\% relative improvements over subword Transformers on CUTE scores, 20%20\% on OCRBench (Liu et al., 2024)).

blocks.html_en: We next investigate how a byte Transformer develops the abstractions that tokenization provides explicitly. By studying an input-copying task on byte models, we find that copying actions need to attend only to certain segmentation positions (not necessarily whitespace), where information from local text pieces can be read out. Based on this finding, we further constrain a range of intermediate layers (up to 25%25\% of all layers) to access only these locally aggregated representations, resembling a global modeling stage over learned local structures. The resulting model retains downstream performance without additional training. This suggests that the apparent hierarchy of local abstraction and global reasoning is not merely imposed by tokenizer-free architectures such as BLT and H-Net, but can also emerge implicitly in the byte Transformer.

sentences.en: We next investigate how a byte Transformer develops the abstractions that tokenization provides explicitly.

By studying an input-copying task on byte models, we find that copying actions need to attend only to certain segmentation positions (not necessarily whitespace), where information from local text pieces can be read out.

Based on this finding, we further constrain a range of intermediate layers (up to 25%25\% of all layers) to access only these locally aggregated representations, resembling a global modeling stage over learned local structures.
The resulting model retains downstream performance without additional training.

This suggests that the apparent hierarchy of local abstraction and global reasoning is not merely imposed by tokenizer-free architectures such as BLT and H-Net, but can also emerge implicitly in the byte Transformer.

blocks.html_en: Finally, we study whether these learned local structures can be exploited during inference. By plotting the per-byte loss distribution, we find that byte Transformers have much higher variance than subword models: many byte positions have near-zero loss (in bits per byte), while substantially larger losses concentrate near the boundaries of the learned local structures. This observation suggests that the extra generation steps are not uniformly expensive in terms of model uncertainty. We therefore apply speculative decoding to construct local structures during inference (Wang et al., 2024; Kallini et al., 2026), and show that a drafting model on byte Transformers can produce 3.4×3.4\times more accepted tokens than on subword Transformers.

sentences.en: Finally, we study whether these learned local structures can be exploited during inference.

By plotting the per-byte loss distribution, we find that byte Transformers have much higher variance than subword models: many byte positions have near-zero loss (in bits per byte), while substantially larger losses concentrate near the boundaries of the learned local structures.
This observation suggests that the extra generation steps are not uniformly expensive in terms of model uncertainty.

We therefore apply speculative decoding to construct local structures during inference (Wang et al., 2024; Kallini et al., 2026), and show that a drafting model on byte Transformers can produce 3.4×3.4\times more accepted tokens than on subword Transformers.

blocks.html_en: To summarize, our results support a simple view of tokenizer-free language modeling: longer byte sequences provide useful additional computation. At the same time, the model can learn useful local abstractions internally rather than relying on a fixed tokenizer. This perspective suggests sequence length, learned abstraction, and computation allocation as closely connected dimensions for future language-model design.

At the same time, the model can learn useful local abstractions internally rather than relying on a fixed tokenizer.
This perspective suggests sequence length, learned abstraction, and computation allocation as closely connected dimensions for future language-model design.

blocks.html_en: 2 Scaling Byte Transformer Language Models

We first ask how the additional tokens in byte sequences affect model quality under parameter and compute constraints. We then examine which task capabilities benefit from byte resolution and how shared depth and sparse capacity change these trade-offs.

blocks.html_en: 2.1 Building Byte Models

We first establish a controlled comparison between byte- and subword-level Transformers. Both models are trained from scratch with a mixed attention model. 11 1 We generally follow the setting of Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026), which interleaves Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025) and Gated Softmax Attention (Qiu et al., 2025) in a 3:13:1 ratio. We occasionally call the architecture flat Transformer, in contrast to architectures with an explicit local-global-local hierarchy. The byte model uses a vocabulary of size 256256, while the subword model uses a 49,15249,152 token vocabulary from the cosmo2-tokenizer (Allal et al., 2025). We use “token” to refer to both byte and subword, depending on the model in context.

blocks.html_en: First, we use token-superposition training (TST; Peng et al., 2026) to improve learning efficiency from the longer byte sequences. blocks.html_en: 3 Emergent Local Abstractions in Byte Transformers

sentences.en: 3 Emergent Local Abstractions in Byte Transformers

blocks.html_en: Tokenization provides explicit local abstractions that can organize text into useful computational units. In this section, we investigate whether similar structures can emerge implicitly in byte Transformers without an explicit tokenizer or hierarchical architecture. We study this question through two complementary experiments. First, we examine how byte models organize information during prediction using an input-copying task. Second, we evaluate whether the representations revealed by this analysis can support alternative computation patterns through a frozen layer intervention.

sentences.en: Tokenization provides explicit local abstractions that can organize text into useful computational units.
In this section, we investigate whether similar structures can emerge implicitly in byte Transformers without an explicit tokenizer or hierarchical architecture.
We study this question through two complementary experiments.
First, we examine how byte models organize information during prediction using an input-copying task.
Second, we evaluate whether the representations revealed by this analysis can support alternative computation patterns through a frozen layer intervention.

blocks.html_en: 3.2 Testing local abstractions with a frozen layer intervention

sentences.en: 3.2 Testing local abstractions with a frozen layer intervention

blocks.html_en: The copying task reveals that multiple byte predictions can repeatedly access a small set of locally aggregated source representations. However, attention patterns alone do not establish whether these representations are sufficient for subsequent computation. We therefore introduce a frozen layer intervention that forces a contiguous range of intermediate layers to operate on a shorter sequence of locally aggregated representations, while preserving full byte-resolution states before and after the intervention. No model parameters are updated.

We therefore introduce a frozen layer intervention that forces a contiguous range of intermediate layers to operate on a shorter sequence of locally aggregated representations, while preserving full byte-resolution states before and after the intervention.

blocks.html_en: Concretely, following the external tokenizer applied in BLT (Pagnoni et al., 2025), we partition the text sequence into local spans using a frozen, architecturally matched 200M Byte model and compress non-image text tokens (for vision–language tasks) by approximately 4×4\times. We treat the selected intermediate layers as a temporary global stage (like the global model in BLT): each local span is mean-pooled into a single representation, processed at the compressed resolution, and then propagated back to the original byte-resolution sequence. This intervention introduces a coarse-grained computation stage into the pretrained Byte-1B model without modifying its parameters or retraining it. More details and results are in Appendix E.2.

blocks.html_en: 4 Information Allocation Along Text Sequences

Locally aggregated representations can support part of Byte’s computation on a shorter sequence (Section 3), while the model still predicts every byte separately. These additional modeling steps raise the question of where the extra computation (Section 2.2) is useful and where it could be reduced. For a given text source, deterministic, reversible tokenizations preserve total entropy (Proposition 1), so finer granularity distributes the same source information over more tokens. We therefore examine how BPB varies across these tokens, how token boundaries explain the distribution gap, and whether small drafts can handle the low-BPB continuations.

blocks.html_en: 5 Related Work
Tokenizer-free language models.

Tokenizer-free language models operate directly on fine-grained inputs such as bytes or characters, avoiding a separately constructed subword vocabulary. ByT5 (Xue et al., 2022) studies byte-to-byte pretraining, while MambaByte (Wang et al., 2024) models byte sequences with selective state-space models. Other works (Clark et al., 2022; YU et al., 2023; Pagnoni et al., 2025; Hwang et al., 2026), introduce hierarchical mechanisms that compress or aggregate fine-grained inputs for coarser-grained computation. In contrast, we study byte language modeling with Transformers with hybrid attention that preserves byte resolution throughout the network.

In contrast, we study byte language modeling with Transformers with hybrid attention that preserves byte resolution throughout the network.

blocks.html_en: Compute scaling and allocation.

Model scale and computation can be varied independently through tokenization and architectural design. Compute Optimal Tokenization (Limisiewicz et al., 2026) studies how token granularity changes the relationship between raw data, sequence length, and compute. Repeated-depth models such as LoopFormer (Jeddi et al., 2026) increase computation while sharing parameters, whereas sparse MoE models such as DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) increase parameter capacity without proportionally increasing activated computation. Building on these directions, we use shared depth to increase Subword computation and sparse experts to reduce Byte activated computation at a given parameter capacity, examining how computation shapes the byte–subword modeling trade-off.

Building on these directions, we use shared depth to increase Subword computation and sparse experts to reduce Byte activated computation at a given parameter capacity, examining how computation shapes the byte–subword modeling trade-off.

blocks.html_en: 6 Discussion and Conclusion

Our results provide a complementary perspective to recent byte-level approaches, which introduce explicit hierarchical or learned tokenization mechanisms to control the cost of long byte sequences. Using a flat Transformer, we show that this sequence-length overhead can instead provide useful computation: byte models benefit from scaling and favor substantially more training data per parameter under a fixed FLOP budget. Moreover, although we do not impose a hierarchy, byte Transformers develop segmentation-like positions that aggregate local text information, and intermediate layers can exploit these representations without loss in downstream performance. This connects flat byte Transformers to hierarchical architectures and suggests that local abstraction and global modeling can emerge implicitly from byte-level training. These learned structures also have inference-time consequences, as prediction difficulty concentrates near their boundaries and can be exploited by speculative decoding. Together, our results suggest that sequence length, learned abstraction, and computation should be viewed as coupled design dimensions, motivating future work on adaptive computation and learned computational granularity for byte language models.

sentences.en: Our results provide a complementary perspective to recent byte-level approaches, which introduce explicit hierarchical or learned tokenization mechanisms to control the cost of long byte sequences.

Using a flat Transformer, we show that this sequence-length overhead can instead provide useful computation: byte models benefit from scaling and favor substantially more training data per parameter under a fixed FLOP budget.

Moreover, although we do not impose a hierarchy, byte Transformers develop segmentation-like positions that aggregate local text information, and intermediate layers can exploit these representations without loss in downstream performance.
This connects flat byte Transformers to hierarchical architectures and suggests that local abstraction and global modeling can emerge implicitly from byte-level training.
These learned structures also have inference-time consequences, as prediction difficulty concentrates near their boundaries and can be exploited by speculative decoding.

Together, our results suggest that sequence length, learned abstraction, and computation should be viewed as coupled design dimensions, motivating future work on adaptive computation and learned computational granularity for byte language models.

blocks.html_en: Limitations

Our study is limited to vanilla Transformer backbones and the evaluated training and task scales; whether the observed scaling behavior and emergent local structures generalize to other architectures, larger models, and broader modalities remains open.

blocks.html_en: Appendix A Architecture and Objectives
A.1 Tokenizers

Our byte tokenizer encodes text directly as UTF-8 without learned merges or Unicode normalization. To support document/chat control and padding within a 256-entry vocabulary, we use 0xC0, 0xC1, and 0xF5–0xFF as special-token IDs. These 13 bytes values are forbidden in UTF-8 and never occur in valid UTF-8 text (Yergeau, 2003).

sentences.en: Our byte tokenizer encodes text directly as UTF-8 without learned merges or Unicode normalization.
To support document/chat control and padding within a 256-entry vocabulary, we use 0xC0, 0xC1, and 0xF5–0xFF as special-token IDs.
These 13 bytes values are forbidden in UTF-8 and never occur in valid UTF-8 text (Yergeau, 2003).

On the pretraining dataset, it averages approximately 4.56 UTF-8 bytes per token. We use this ratio in the compute and data exposure calculations in Section 2.2 and Appendices C.

blocks.html_en: A.2 Token-Superposition Training (TST)

Let Ti,jT_{i,j} be the jjth token in bag BiB_{i}. Each bag is represented by the average of its token embeddings, including causal hash features when enabled.

blocks.html_en: A.4 Dense model configuration

All models are trained from scratch with untied input and output embeddings.

blocks.html_en: This appendix describes training for the main model suite: the 200M–3B Byte and Subword models evaluated on CUTE, QA RC, and vision–language benchmarks in Section 2.3, together with the looped and MoE models compared in Section 2.4.

blocks.html_en: B.1 Pretraining hyperparameters

All model families are pretrained on ClimbMix (Diao et al., 2025). The 16-, 20-, 24-, 28-, and 40-layer models use 50k, 60k, 70k, 80k, and 100k updates, respectively. The byte sequence length is four times the subword sequence length; with the batch sizes in Table 7, the two families process approximately the same amount of source text per update during ordinary next-token training. Because byte and subword models also use the same number of updates at each scale, their total source-text exposure under this training regime is approximately matched.

We evaluate CUTE (Appendix D.3) after SFT for both byte and subword models. Language-modeling and QA RC evaluations use base models. blocks.html_en: B.3 Vision–language training details
Architecture.

We adapt Byte and Subword models into vision–language models (VLMs) using an identical vision–language architecture. A frozen SigLIP2 SO400M vision encoder connects to the pretrained language model through a two-layer GELU MLP projector, which maps visual representations into the language embedding space. The projected visual tokens enter the language sequence through a unified image-token interface.

sentences.en: We adapt Byte and Subword models into vision–language models (VLMs) using an identical vision–language architecture.
A frozen SigLIP2 SO400M vision encoder connects to the pretrained language model through a two-layer GELU MLP projector, which maps visual representations into the language embedding space.
The projected visual tokens enter the language sequence through a unified image-token interface.

blocks.html_en: Training.

We use a two-stage training pipeline following the standard LLaVA recipe. Stage 1 trains only the projector on LLaVA-Pretrain, keeping the vision encoder and language model frozen, with learning rate 10−310^{-3} and effective batch size 256. Stage 2 jointly fine-tunes the projector and language model on LLaVA-NeXT-SFT, keeping the vision encoder frozen, with learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} and effective batch size 128. Both stages use AdamW, bfloat16 mixed precision, 3% warmup followed by cosine learning-rate decay, and one training epoch.

C.1 Sweep settings

The IsoFLOPs sweep builds on the pretraining setup in Appendix B.1 and uses the BPB evaluation protocol in Appendix D.1. We evaluate dense byte and subword models under four recipes: raw, hash-only, TST-only, and TST+hash. To cover the optimal model sizes at low FLOP budgets, we extend the dense configurations in Table 5 down to 8 layers. For each model size, the number of training updates is determined by the FLOP budget, replacing the prescribed update counts of the main model suite. Warmup lasts 1,000 updates instead of 1% of training; the remaining training hyperparameters, including decay over the final 20% of updates, follow Table 7. Architecture and enabled TST/hash components use the settings in Table 4. Figure 6 presents the complete IsoFLOPs sweep results across all evaluated model sizes and FLOP budgets.

blocks.html_en: D.4 Vision–language evaluation

We evaluate with the lmms-eval framework (Zhang et al., 2025) on vision–language benchmarks covering several capabilities. DocVQA (Mathew et al., 2021), OCRBench, TextVQA, and ChartQA (Masry et al., 2022) assess OCR and document understanding; ScienceQA-IMG (Lu et al., 2022) and MMBench (Liu et al., 2025) assess knowledge-intensive visual reasoning. MME (Fu et al., 2025), GQA (Hudson and Manning, 2019), and POPE (Li et al., 2023) assess general visual understanding, covering object hallucination, visual question answering, and perception and cognition.

blocks.html_en: Table 13 and Table 14 show that performance on the remaining vision–language tasks is more task-dependent than on OCRBench and TextVQA. Across both dense and MoE models, the differences between Byte and Subword are mixed at smaller scales, but generally become more favorable to Byte as model scale or capacity increases. For the largest dense models, Byte surpasses Subword on ScienceQA-IMG, MMBench, and POPE and nearly matches it on GQA, while the largest Byte MoE model achieves higher scores on several broader vision–language benchmarks, including ScienceQA-IMG, MMBench, MME, and GQA. Together with the consistent gains on OCRBench and TextVQA reported in Table 1, these results suggest that the clearest advantage of byte-level modeling appears on fine-grained vision–language tasks, while broader vision–language capabilities become increasingly competitive with scale and capacity.

For the largest dense models, Byte surpasses Subword on ScienceQA-IMG, MMBench, and POPE and nearly matches it on GQA, while the largest Byte MoE model achieves higher scores on several broader vision–language benchmarks, including ScienceQA-IMG, MMBench, MME, and GQA.

Together with the consistent gains on OCRBench and TextVQA reported in Table 1, these results suggest that the clearest advantage of byte-level modeling appears on fine-grained vision–language tasks, while broader vision–language capabilities become increasingly competitive with scale and capacity.

blocks.html_en: H-Net target filtering.

H-Net’s highest BPB values concentrate on TAB (0x09), LF (0x0A), CR (0x0D), { (0x7B), and } (0x7D). H-Net were trained on FineWeb-Edu, a filtered subset of FineWeb. FineWeb’s C4 filter rejects an entire document when a surviving line contains {, also removing any paired } in that document. It drops empty lines and joins retained lines with a single LF, while text extraction collapses whitespace such as TAB and CR. These preprocessing choices may explain the extreme BPB values through reduced training exposure to braces, TAB, CR, and repeated line breaks.

We test the sensitivity of BPB aggregation to tokenizer choice using Byte-1B and BLT-1B. For each model, we average BPB over complete spans defined by the Subword, Qwen3, and Qwen3.5 tokenizers and assign the span mean to each constituent byte. The aggregated distributions are similar across the three tokenizers (Figure 13).

blocks.html_en: Uniform four-byte grouping.

To test whether average span length alone explains the aggregated distribution, we also use non-overlapping four-byte groups, close to Subword’s average token length in bytes. For both byte models, uniform grouping reduces variation but leaves more near-zero mass and less far-tail mass than tokenizer grouping (Figure 13). These differences highlight the role of tokenizer boundaries in shaping the aggregated BPB distribution.

blocks.html_en: Implications for speculative decoding.

The drafting experiment provides a proof of concept for computation allocation at inference. Longer byte agreement runs indicate that small drafts can match their targets across many consecutive byte tokens in reference text. These runs provide a teacher-forced diagnostic of drafting opportunities. Generated histories may differ from the reference text, so these lengths do not provide a general upper bound on accepted draft length during generation. In speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023), accepted tokens become part of the subsequent context, and each round includes correction or bonus outputs. Establishing practical speedups therefore requires decoding along generated histories with finite proposals and measuring the costs of drafting and target verification.

抽象的

Tokenizer-free language models remove the inductive bias of fixed tokenizers by modeling text directly as bytes, but the resulting longer sequences substantially increase computation and eliminate explicit text abstractions. We ask whether this additional computation can be useful, and whether standard Transformers can learn the abstractions that tokenization provides. We study these questions on Transformers without specialized tokenization-related architectures. With token-superposition training and hash embeddings, byte Transformers consistently outperform subword Transformers as model size scales. We further find that byte Transformers build local text abstractions as external tokenizers: a set of segmentation-like positions are used to collect local context representations, and restricting up to 25%25\% of intermediate layers to these local representations preserves downstream performance. Finally, these learned structures induce highly non-uniform generation difficulty, with uncertainty concentrated near local structure boundaries; exploiting them for speculative decoding yields 3.4×3.4\times more accepted tokens than in subword Transformers.

1 Introduction

Tokenizer-free language models, or byte language models, aim to remove externally imposed tokenizers by modeling text directly as byte sequences (Xue et al., 2022; YU et al., 2023; Slagle, 2024; Tsiamas et al., 2025; Shah et al., 2026). This formulation provides a universal input space and a new joint learning setting. However, it also introduces two main challenges. First, byte sequences are longer than subword sequences. If a typical subword contains K (usually around 4) bytes, a byte model must process K times more sequence positions. Second, prior studies suggest that effective language modeling benefits from prior abstractions over raw text. Directly modeling bytes can therefore underperform tokenized models, despite having a more general input representation.

Recent works (BLT Pagnoni et al., 2025, H-Net Hwang et al., 2026, ByteFlow Deng et al., 2026) develop new network architectures with built-in tokenization mechanisms. For example, in BLT, local encoder layers first encode byte streams into variable-sized chunks, then global layers operate on the chunks, and local decoder layers decode chunks back to bytes. While these architectures demonstrate the promise of joint tokenization, they often need specialized training and optimization strategies, making it less clear how much of the observed gains are from the joint formulation. In this work, we retain the flat Transformer architecture (without the explicit local-global-local hierarchy) and investigate the two challenges underlying byte-level language modeling: Can the additional computation caused by longer sequences be beneficial, and how does a Transformer recover useful text abstractions directly from bytes?

We study the scaling behavior of byte Transformers, and the main findings are: 1) with two modeling ingredients (token-superposition training (Peng et al., 2026) and hash embeddings), byte Transformers consistently outperform subword Transformers when scaling the number of parameters (Figure 1a). 2) Byte models remain effective as training data continues to scale. Given a fixed FLOPs budget (Figure 1c), the optimal proportion between data and parameters is around 1.5 to 3 times that of subword models. These results motivate a different perspective on sequence length: rather than treating longer sequences as a defect, they can provide additional computation under the same parameter budget, which is a useful scaling axis for language models. Further evaluations on downstream text-only and vision–language tasks show that byte Transformers significantly improve performance on tasks that require fine-grained perception (around 40%40\% relative improvements over subword Transformers on CUTE scores, 20%20\% on OCRBench (Liu et al., 2024)).

We next investigate how a byte Transformer develops the abstractions that tokenization provides explicitly. By studying an input-copying task on byte models, we find that copying actions need to attend only to certain segmentation positions (not necessarily whitespace), where information from local text pieces can be read out. Based on this finding, we further constrain a range of intermediate layers (up to 25%25\% of all layers) to access only these locally aggregated representations, resembling a global modeling stage over learned local structures. The resulting model retains downstream performance without additional training. This suggests that the apparent hierarchy of local abstraction and global reasoning is not merely imposed by tokenizer-free architectures such as BLT and H-Net, but can also emerge implicitly in the byte Transformer.

Finally, we study whether these learned local structures can be exploited during inference. By plotting the per-byte loss distribution, we find that byte Transformers have much higher variance than subword models: many byte positions have near-zero loss (in bits per byte), while substantially larger losses concentrate near the boundaries of the learned local structures. This observation suggests that the extra generation steps are not uniformly expensive in terms of model uncertainty. We therefore apply speculative decoding to construct local structures during inference (Wang et al., 2024; Kallini et al., 2026), and show that a drafting model on byte Transformers can produce 3.4×3.4\times more accepted tokens than on subword Transformers.

To summarize, our results support a simple view of tokenizer-free language modeling: longer byte sequences provide useful additional computation. At the same time, the model can learn useful local abstractions internally rather than relying on a fixed tokenizer. This perspective suggests sequence length, learned abstraction, and computation allocation as closely connected dimensions for future language-model design.

2 Scaling Byte Transformer Language Models

We first ask how the additional tokens in byte sequences affect model quality under parameter and compute constraints. We then examine which task capabilities benefit from byte resolution and how shared depth and sparse capacity change these trade-offs.

2.1 Building Byte Models

We first establish a controlled comparison between byte- and subword-level Transformers. Both models are trained from scratch with a mixed attention model. 11 1 We generally follow the setting of Qwen3.5 (Qwen Team, 2026), which interleaves Gated DeltaNet (Yang et al., 2025) and Gated Softmax Attention (Qiu et al., 2025) in a 3:13:1 ratio. We occasionally call the architecture flat Transformer, in contrast to architectures with an explicit local-global-local hierarchy. The byte model uses a vocabulary of size 256256, while the subword model uses a 49,15249,152 token vocabulary from the cosmo2-tokenizer (Allal et al., 2025). We use “token” to refer to both byte and subword, depending on the model in context.

Directly applying the standard training recipe to bytes is suboptimal. Byte sequences contain substantially more tokens, while each byte token carries less local semantic context than a subword token. We find the following two ingredients are effective for training byte models.

First, we use token-superposition training (TST; Peng et al., 2026) to improve learning efficiency from the longer byte sequences. TST averages four consecutive token embeddings and predicts the corresponding next four-token bag. Applying TST during the first 30% of training provides 4×4\times token exposure in this stage, while reverting to standard next-token prediction for the remaining 70% results in 1.9×1.9\times total text exposure under the same number of training tokens (see Appendix A.2 for details).

Second, we augment byte embeddings with hash embeddings as (Pagnoni et al., 2025). The model learns representations for nn-grams of bytes and combines them with byte embeddings, allowing each byte token to incorporate information from nearby multi-byte patterns (Appendix A.3). Similarly, we increase the convolution width of gated DeltaNet from 44 (for subword models) to 1616 (for byte models), to build a broader local receptive field.

Unless otherwise specified, byte models apply TST and hash embeddings (denoted by Byte), while subword models don’t (denoted by Subword). We later ablate these components to separate the contribution of the training recipe from that of input granularity.

2.2 Parameter and Compute Efficiency under IsoFLOPs

A longer byte sequence can be viewed either as a computational burden or as an opportunity to allocate more computation to a model with the same number of parameters. To distinguish these effects, we study how byte and subword Transformers scale along three coupled axes: model size, data exposure, and training compute.

Following the standard practice of model scaling analyses, we train families of byte and subword models with different training FLOPs per token MM and cumulative training data volume VV (measured in bytes consumed during training), record their validation loss LL (measured in bits per byte, BPB), and fit the loss LL as function of MM and VV. We adapt the Chinchilla law (Hoffmann et al., 2022),

L⁡(M,V)=E+A​M−α+B​V−β,L(M,V)=E+AM^{-\alpha}+BV^{-\beta}, (1)

where α,β,E,A,B\alpha,\beta,E,A,B are fiting coefficients. We also denote total training FLOPs C=M​DC=MD, where DD is the amount of training data in tokens. 22 2 A subword token or TST bag can represent multiple source bytes, so we account for this using V=s​DV=sD, with varying average source bytes per token ss.

Following Hoffmann et al. (2022), we compare model performance in the compute-optimal manner. Given a FLOPs budget CC, we collect loss LL of models with various sizes NN (or equally, MM) under CC, fit a curve for the obtained (N,L)(N,L) pairs, and the optimal parameter count under the FLOPs budget N⋆​(C)N^{\star}(C) is located at the minimum loss L⋆L^{\star} (see Figure 6 and Appendix C for details). Similarly, we obtain the optimal training byte volume V⋆​(C)V^{\star}(C). By varying CC, we trace the L⋆L^{\star}–N⋆N^{\star} and L⋆L^{\star}–CC Pareto frontiers in Figure 1.

Byte has lower optimal loss at the same optimal parameter count

The L⋆L^{\star}–N⋆N^{\star} Pareto frontiers (Figure 1a) of Byte consistently below Subword. It suggests that Transformers can transform additional computation to performance gains. Meanwhile, Figure 1b shows a different story: under the same FLOPs budgets, Subword is always better. We defer discussion on scaling along computation to Section 2.4.

Byte optima allocate more source bytes per parameter.

Compared with Subword, at the same training-compute budgets, the fitted optima select smaller Byte models and generally allocate more (3.2×3.2\times) source bytes per parameter (Figure 1c). It implies that Byte can reach lower BPB if training data continues to scale.

TST and hashing embeddings provide larger combined gains for Byte.

We ablate TST and hashing at matched depth and training compute within each family. Combining them consistently improves BPB over raw training, with larger gains for Byte.

2.3 Fine-Grained Capabilities in Text-Only and Vision–Language Tasks

We next examine whether the modeling advantages of byte-level representations translate into downstream text-only and vision-language tasks. 33 3 For Section 2.3 and 2.4, we use a separate main model suite spanning 200M–3B sizes, instead of the IsoFLOPs sweep settings in Section 2.2. At each parameter scale, Byte and Subword use the same number of updates and approximately the same source-text exposure. See Appendix B for detailed settings. 44 4 We train vision-language models in the LLaVA style (Liu et al., 2023) with backbone language models replaced by Byte. Training details are given in Appendix B.3. We evaluate word manipulation with CUTE (Edman et al., 2024), and fine-grained OCR tasks with OCRBench and TextVQA (Singh et al., 2019).

The results in Table 1 show that Byte has a clear advantage in word manipulation capabilities over Subword. We think the better fine-grained modeling ability of Byte comes from stronger perception of inputs and stronger ability to generate byte-level sequences. We particularly expect better alignment among modalities in future byte language model-based multimodality learning.

We additionally evaluate both model families on broader standard text-only (2121 tasks, Table 9) and vision-language benchmarks (55 tasks, Table 13) in Appendix D. On text tasks, Byte model consistently outputperforms Subword, due to more computation per parameter. On vision-language tasks, Byte is on par with Subword.

2.4 Controlling Computation with Shared Depth and Sparse Experts

The preceding results reveal a compute–quality trade-off between Byte and Subword. We therefore examine two complementary ways to shift this trade-off (Figure 2): increasing Subword computation through shared depth, and reducing Byte’s activated computation at a given parameter capacity with sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE). Using the main model suite, we evaluate four-pass Subword models and Byte MoE models under the training schedules of their dense counterparts; architecture details are provided in Appendix A.

Increasing computation through shared depth.

We follow the setting of LoopFormer (Jeddi et al., 2026) to increase Subword computation with four shared backbone passes. It closes most of the BPB gap to Byte in both the parameter and compute views, showing that repeated depth is an effective way to scale computation for subword models. The looped Subword models also achieve consistently higher QA RC than the standard dense Byte models across the evaluated scales.

Reducing activated computation with sparse experts.

Sparse MoE (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) consistently improves Byte BPB in both the parameter and compute views, showing that sparse activation is an effective way to reduce computation while retaining larger model capacity. Notably, the 1B Byte MoE achieves lower BPB than the 3B dense Subword model while reaching comparable QA RC.

Together, these results show that the byte–subword modeling gap depends strongly on how computation is allocated. Increasing computation through shared depth allows Subword models to recover much of the BPB gap, while sparse activation improves the compute efficiency of Byte models at comparable parameter capacity.

3 Emergent Local Abstractions in Byte Transformers

Tokenization provides explicit local abstractions that can organize text into useful computational units. In this section, we investigate whether similar structures can emerge implicitly in byte Transformers without an explicit tokenizer or hierarchical architecture. We study this question through two complementary experiments. First, we examine how byte models organize information during prediction using an input-copying task. Second, we evaluate whether the representations revealed by this analysis can support alternative computation patterns through a frozen layer intervention.

3.1 Copying as a probe of local information structure

To probe how text semantics are abstracted and accessed in models, we study the copying task by prompting the model with “Your task is to copy the string: XX. Now copy it: XX”, where XX is a short string composed of multiple meaningful English words. We evaluate Byte-1B by analyzing attention patterns during the copying process, focusing on how different layers access the source text when generating the copied sequence (see Appendix E.1 for details).

As shown in Figure 3, Byte-1B exhibits a clear attention aggregation pattern during copying. In particular, attention in intermediate layers becomes concentrated on a small set of source positions that are repeatedly accessed by multiple consecutive target bytes. This aggregation occurs even without any whitespace in inputs, indicating that it does not simply arise from explicit separators. 55 5 Whitespaces may provide shortcuts during the aggregation: model can learn to utilize repeatedly appearing tokens, ablation of separators is in Figure 9. The repeated reuse of these positions suggests that the byte model internally develops a mechanism for consolidating local information into representative states, providing an implicit structure over the byte sequence.

3.2 Testing local abstractions with a frozen layer intervention

The copying task reveals that multiple byte predictions can repeatedly access a small set of locally aggregated source representations. However, attention patterns alone do not establish whether these representations are sufficient for subsequent computation. We therefore introduce a frozen layer intervention that forces a contiguous range of intermediate layers to operate on a shorter sequence of locally aggregated representations, while preserving full byte-resolution states before and after the intervention. No model parameters are updated.

Concretely, following the external tokenizer applied in BLT (Pagnoni et al., 2025), we partition the text sequence into local spans using a frozen, architecturally matched 200M Byte model and compress non-image text tokens (for vision–language tasks) by approximately 4×4\times. We treat the selected intermediate layers as a temporary global stage (like the global model in BLT): each local span is mean-pooled into a single representation, processed at the compressed resolution, and then propagated back to the original byte-resolution sequence. This intervention introduces a coarse-grained computation stage into the pretrained Byte-1B model without modifying its parameters or retraining it. More details and results are in Appendix E.2.

We apply the same intervention to Byte-1B and Subword-1B across several downstream tasks, sweeping the start and end layers of the compressed global stage GG. As shown in Figure 4, Byte exhibits a clear recovery in performance when the global stage is placed sufficiently late in the network, with the trend becoming apparent for intervals starting around layer 17. More importantly, a stable compressible region emerges in the later layers: for G=[21,27]G=[21,27], 7 of the model’s 28 layers (25%) operate only on the compressed local representations, while downstream performance remains close to the uncompressed baseline across tasks. In contrast, applying the same intervention to the subword model causes substantial degradation across nearly all layer intervals. This contrast suggests that the robustness to an intermediate compressed global stage is a property of the byte model rather than a generic consequence of pooling hidden states.

4 Information Allocation Along Text Sequences

Locally aggregated representations can support part of Byte’s computation on a shorter sequence (Section 3), while the model still predicts every byte separately. These additional modeling steps raise the question of where the extra computation (Section 2.2) is useful and where it could be reduced. For a given text source, deterministic, reversible tokenizations preserve total entropy (Proposition 1), so finer granularity distributes the same source information over more tokens. We therefore examine how BPB varies across these tokens, how token boundaries explain the distribution gap, and whether small drafts can handle the low-BPB continuations.

Near zero, byte densities approach 1/x1/x, with fitted power-law exponent α∈[−0.97,−0.91]\alpha\in[-0.97,-0.91], whereas subword densities are shallower, with α∈[−0.8,−0.6]\alpha\in[-0.8,-0.6] (Figure 5a–b). Together, these patterns show that Byte has more probability mass at both low and high BPB than Subword (Figure 5b–c; Table 2). We also verify this law in public byte models, including BLT and H-Net, and widely used subword models. The byte models have nearly overlapping BPB distributions (Figure 11; Table 15).

Token boundaries explain the distribution gap.

We aggregate Byte BPB by averaging within each token span defined by a subword tokenizer. The aggregated distribution (dotted lines in Figure 5b–c) closely matches the native Subword distribution.77 7 We also ablated boundaries from the Qwen3 and Qwen3.5 tokenizers, which yielded similar aggregated distributions (Figure 13; Appendix F.3). This result indicates that the distribution gap largely reflects how information is grouped into tokens. Subword tokenization provides a statistical prior for this grouping: it combines high-BPB bytes with predictable continuations into fewer tokens, reducing near-zero BPB mass while retaining the source’s total information (Proposition 1).

Byte modeling can allocate more computation to difficult tokens.

For the same total source information, Byte uses multiple modeling steps within a span that Subword handles in one step, retaining high-BPB bytes as separate tokens (Figure 5c). This supports the argument in Section 2.2 that longer sequences can scale computation without increasing model size.

4.2 Drafting Low-BPB Continuations

Maintaining a fixed byte granularity allows more computation for high-BPB tokens, but also adds modeling steps for the many low-BPB continuations (Figure 5; Table 2). We therefore examine whether speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023) can reduce this overhead.

We use existing 200M and 50M models as drafts and same-family 1B models as targets for both Byte and Subword. We do not train specialized drafts. On the validation dataset, we compare accepted bytes per target forward pass in an oracle simulation on the given evaluation text. Appendix G specifies the protocol.

Higher byte acceptance rates compensate for shorter token spans.

At both draft sizes, Byte accepts about 3.4×3.4\times as many tokens per target forward pass as Subword. Accepted bytes per forward are nearly identical with 200M drafts and slightly higher for Byte with 50M drafts (Table 3). The 200M drafts yield longer accepted text per forward in both families.

These acceptance lengths suggest that many additional byte tokens can be verified together, reducing the need for separate sequential target calls. The comparable text coverage of the two families at both draft sizes suggests that joint verification could offset much of the extra sequential overhead introduced by byte granularity.

5 Related Work

Tokenizer-free language models.

Tokenizer-free language models operate directly on fine-grained inputs such as bytes or characters, avoiding a separately constructed subword vocabulary. ByT5 (Xue et al., 2022) studies byte-to-byte pretraining, while MambaByte (Wang et al., 2024) models byte sequences with selective state-space models. Other works (Clark et al., 2022; YU et al., 2023; Pagnoni et al., 2025; Hwang et al., 2026), introduce hierarchical mechanisms that compress or aggregate fine-grained inputs for coarser-grained computation. In contrast, we study byte language modeling with Transformers with hybrid attention that preserves byte resolution throughout the network.

Compute scaling and allocation.

Model scale and computation can be varied independently through tokenization and architectural design. Compute Optimal Tokenization (Limisiewicz et al., 2026) studies how token granularity changes the relationship between raw data, sequence length, and compute. Repeated-depth models such as LoopFormer (Jeddi et al., 2026) increase computation while sharing parameters, whereas sparse MoE models such as DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025) increase parameter capacity without proportionally increasing activated computation. Building on these directions, we use shared depth to increase Subword computation and sparse experts to reduce Byte activated computation at a given parameter capacity, examining how computation shapes the byte–subword modeling trade-off.

6 Discussion and Conclusion

Our results provide a complementary perspective to recent byte-level approaches, which introduce explicit hierarchical or learned tokenization mechanisms to control the cost of long byte sequences. Using a flat Transformer, we show that this sequence-length overhead can instead provide useful computation: byte models benefit from scaling and favor substantially more training data per parameter under a fixed FLOP budget. Moreover, although we do not impose a hierarchy, byte Transformers develop segmentation-like positions that aggregate local text information, and intermediate layers can exploit these representations without loss in downstream performance. This connects flat byte Transformers to hierarchical architectures and suggests that local abstraction and global modeling can emerge implicitly from byte-level training. These learned structures also have inference-time consequences, as prediction difficulty concentrates near their boundaries and can be exploited by speculative decoding. Together, our results suggest that sequence length, learned abstraction, and computation should be viewed as coupled design dimensions, motivating future work on adaptive computation and learned computational granularity for byte language models.

局限性

Our study is limited to vanilla Transformer backbones and the evaluated training and task scales; whether the observed scaling behavior and emergent local structures generalize to other architectures, larger models, and broader modalities remains open.

Statement on the Use of Generative AI

In this work, we used generative AI tools to assist with experimental design, method implementation and debugging, training and mathematical exposition. We also used these tools for literature retrieval, figure and table preparation, and manuscript drafting and editing. We take full responsibility for the final manuscript and associated artifacts, including AI-assisted text, code, analyses, and claims.

Reproducibility Statement

We provide model configurations, training hyperparameters, and evaluation settings for the main model suite and IsoFLOPs sweep in Appendices A–D. Settings for BPB distribution analyses and experiments on draft acceptance and local information structure are detailed in Appendices E–G.

Appendix A Architecture and Objectives

A.1 Tokenizers

Our byte tokenizer encodes text directly as UTF-8 without learned merges or Unicode normalization. To support document/chat control and padding within a 256-entry vocabulary, we use 0xC0, 0xC1, and 0xF5–0xFF as special-token IDs. These 13 bytes values are forbidden in UTF-8 and never occur in valid UTF-8 text (Yergeau, 2003).

For subword models, we use HuggingFaceTB/cosmo2-tokenizer (Allal et al., 2025)88 8 https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceTB/cosmo2-tokenizer, a pretrained byte-level BPE tokenizer with 49,152 vocabulary entries. On the pretraining dataset, it averages approximately 4.56 UTF-8 bytes per token. We use this ratio in the compute and data exposure calculations in Section 2.2 and Appendices C.

A.2 Token-Superposition Training (TST)

TST (Peng et al., 2026) lets each model input represent several tokens. We divide a token sequence 𝐓\mathbf{T} into non-overlapping bags of K=4K=4 consecutive tokens, forming the sequence 𝐁=(B1,…,B|𝐓|/K)\mathbf{B}=(B_{1},\ldots,B_{|\mathbf{T}|/K}). Let Ti,jT_{i,j} be the jjth token in bag BiB_{i}. Each bag is represented by the average of its token embeddings, including causal hash features when enabled.

The causal model and its single output head, with parameters θ\theta, use the preceding bags 𝐁<i\mathbf{B}_{<i} to produce one shared token distribution pθ(⋅∣𝐁<i)p_{\theta}(\cdot\mid\mathbf{B}_{<i}) for all tokens in the next bag BiB_{i}. The loss averages token cross-entropy over all target bags (Peng et al., 2026, Eq. (3)):

ℒTST(𝐁;θ)=−1|𝐓|−K∑i=2|𝐓|/K∑j=1Klnpθ(Ti,j∣𝐁<i).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{TST}}(\mathbf{B};\theta)=-\frac{1}{|\mathbf{T}|-K}\sum_{i=2}^{|\mathbf{T}|/K}\sum_{j=1}^{K}\ln p_{\theta}(T_{i,j}\mid\mathbf{B}_{<i}). (5)

The first 30% of pretraining updates use TST; the remaining 70% use ordinary next-token training on the same parameters. During TST, each four-token bag counts as one training token. With a fixed number of training tokens per update, this schedule provides 0.3×4+0.7×1=1.90.3\times 4+0.7\times 1=1.9 times the text exposure of ordinary next-token training at the same training-token count.

A.3 Hashed Embeddings

To supply local context at the input, we augment token embeddings with hashed nn-gram representations inspired by BLT (Pagnoni et al., 2025). For a sequence x1:Tx_{1:T} of byte or subword tokens, let 𝒢\mathcal{G} denote the set of nn-gram groups, indexed by their lengths. The input representation is

ei=11+|𝒢|[E(xi)+∑n∈𝒢En(Hash(xi−n+1:i))].e_{i}=\frac{1}{1+|\mathcal{G}|}\left[E(x_{i})+\sum_{n\in\mathcal{G}}E_{n}\!\left(\operatorname{Hash}(x_{i-n+1:i})\right)\right]. (6)

Here EE is the ordinary token embedding table, and EnE_{n} is a separate embedding table for length nn, indexed by the shared polynomial hash Hash\operatorname{Hash}. When i<ni<n, the missing left context is padded with zeros.

For Byte, 𝒢={5,6,7,8}\mathcal{G}=\{5,6,7,8\}, with four hash tables of 32,768 slots each. For Subword, 𝒢={2}\mathcal{G}=\{2\}, with one hash table of 131,072 slots. Both families therefore use 131,072 hash slots in total.

A.4 Dense model configuration

We scale the Qwen3.5 text architecture (Qwen Team, 2026) using the dense configurations in Table 5. Its hybrid attention combines Gated DeltaNet (GDN) and Gated Softmax Attention (Qiu et al., 2025) in a 3:1 ratio. We increase depth in four-layer increments to preserve this ratio. All models are trained from scratch with untied input and output embeddings.

We use NN for the number of unique active model parameters, including the output embedding. Input/hash embeddings are excluded. The difference in NN between Subword and Byte models comes mainly from the larger subword output embedding, with a smaller contribution from their convolution widths.

A.5 MoE configuration

Hidden widths and attention configurations follow Table 5. All layers use MoE, and the expert widths in Table 6 apply to both routed and shared experts. Each layer uses 8 active experts selected from 64 routed experts, together with 1 shared expert. For MoE models, NN denotes the active parameter count: it includes routers, selected routed experts, and shared experts, and excludes inactive routed experts. NtotalN_{\mathrm{total}} counts all model parameters except hash embeddings.

We use the auxiliary-loss-free load balancing strategy of DeepSeek-V3 (DeepSeek-AI et al., 2025). For a hidden state hh, the router computes token-to-expert affinities se=σ⁡(we⊤​h)s_{e}=\sigma(w_{e}^{\top}h), where wew_{e} is the router vector for expert ee. Each routed expert has a bias beb_{e}, initialized to zero. The eight experts with the largest se+bes_{e}+b_{e} form the selected set 𝒦⁡(h)\mathcal{K}(h). The selected experts are combined with weights

αe=2.5​se∑j∈𝒦⁡(h)sj,MoE⁡(h)=fshared​(h)+∑e∈𝒦⁡(h)αe​fe​(h).\alpha_{e}=\frac{2.5s_{e}}{\sum_{j\in\mathcal{K}(h)}s_{j}},\qquad\operatorname{MoE}(h)=f_{\mathrm{shared}}(h)+\sum_{e\in\mathcal{K}(h)}\alpha_{e}f_{e}(h). (7)

The bias affects expert selection, while the gating weights are computed from the original affinities ses_{e}. After each training step, we update the biases according to

be←be+γ​sign⁡(n¯−ne),b_{e}\leftarrow b_{e}+\gamma\operatorname{sign}(\bar{n}-n_{e}), (8)

where nen_{e} is the number of token assignments to expert ee across the whole training batch, n¯\bar{n} is the mean count over routed experts, and γ\gamma is the bias update speed. We use γ=10−3\gamma=10^{-3} and freeze the biases during the final 5% of training updates.

A.6 Looped model configuration

LoopFormer (Jeddi et al., 2026) repeatedly applies a shared Transformer stack, conditioning each pass on normalized time and step size. It combines next-token prediction on full and shorter trajectories with a shortcut-consistency objective to support elastic-depth inference.

Our looped Subword control adopts the shared-stack recurrence with four fixed passes, retaining the baseline decoder blocks and ordinary next-token objective. Let H(0)H^{(0)} denote the input token embeddings and Φθ\Phi_{\theta} the complete causal decoder stack with parameters θ\theta. The recurrence is

H(r)=Φθ(H(r−1)),r=1,…,4.H^{(r)}=\Phi_{\theta}\!\left(H^{(r-1)}\right),\qquad r=1,\ldots,4. (9)

Both training and evaluation use this recurrence, with a single prediction head after the final pass. Training compute includes all four decoder passes and one output-head application, with forward and backward matrix operations counted as six FLOPs per participating weight per processed token. NN counts each shared parameter once.

Appendix B Main Model Suite: Training Details

This appendix describes training for the main model suite: the 200M–3B Byte and Subword models evaluated on CUTE, QA RC, and vision–language benchmarks in Section 2.3, together with the looped and MoE models compared in Section 2.4.

B.1 Pretraining hyperparameters

All model families are pretrained on ClimbMix (Diao et al., 2025). The 16-, 20-, 24-, 28-, and 40-layer models use 50k, 60k, 70k, 80k, and 100k updates, respectively. The byte sequence length is four times the subword sequence length; with the batch sizes in Table 7, the two families process approximately the same amount of source text per update during ordinary next-token training. Because byte and subword models also use the same number of updates at each scale, their total source-text exposure under this training regime is approximately matched.

We use μ\muP-style hyperparameter transfer (Yang et al., 2021), with the following width and batch corrections in our Muon/AdamW optimizer (Jordan et al., 2024; Loshchilov and Hutter, 2017). Let η0\eta_{0} be the common base learning rate in Table 7 and d0=768d_{0}=768 the reference width. Let rr and cc denote the numbers of rows and columns, respectively, of a parameter matrix updated by Muon. The peak learning rates for AdamW and Muon are

ηAdam\displaystyle\eta_{\mathrm{Adam}} =η0​2​d0/d,\displaystyle=\eta_{0}\sqrt{2}\sqrt{d_{0}/d}, (10)
ηMuon​(r,c)\displaystyle\eta_{\mathrm{Muon}}(r,c) =η0​2​max⁡(1,r/c).\displaystyle=\eta_{0}\sqrt{2}\sqrt{\max(1,r/c)}.

The factor 2\sqrt{2} comes from learning-rate scaling with batch size. We neither tune nor automatically scale the global batch size, so this factor remains constant across model scales. Our pretraining hyperparameter settings are largely based on nanochat99 9 https://github.com/karpathy/nanochat.

B.2 Text supervised fine-tuning

We evaluate CUTE (Appendix D.3) after SFT for both byte and subword models. Language-modeling and QA RC evaluations use base models. The SFT mixture combines Smol-SmolTalk (Allal et al., 2025), MMLU, GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), and CUTE-style tasks, with loss on assistant responses. SFT starts at 0.8 of the pretraining learning rate, with 10% warmup steps and decay to zero over the final 50% of updates.

B.3 Vision–language training details

建筑学。

We adapt Byte and Subword models into vision–language models (VLMs) using an identical vision–language architecture. A frozen SigLIP2 SO400M vision encoder connects to the pretrained language model through a two-layer GELU MLP projector, which maps visual representations into the language embedding space. The projected visual tokens enter the language sequence through a unified image-token interface.

Training.

We use a two-stage training pipeline following the standard LLaVA recipe. Stage 1 trains only the projector on LLaVA-Pretrain, keeping the vision encoder and language model frozen, with learning rate 10−310^{-3} and effective batch size 256. Stage 2 jointly fine-tunes the projector and language model on LLaVA-NeXT-SFT, keeping the vision encoder frozen, with learning rate 2×10−52\times 10^{-5} and effective batch size 128. Both stages use AdamW, bfloat16 mixed precision, 3% warmup followed by cosine learning-rate decay, and one training epoch.

Appendix C IsoFLOPs Sweep Details

C.1 Sweep settings

The IsoFLOPs sweep builds on the pretraining setup in Appendix B.1 and uses the BPB evaluation protocol in Appendix D.1. We evaluate dense byte and subword models under four recipes: raw, hash-only, TST-only, and TST+hash. E.1 Input-copying Task Setting

Prompt and input variants.

Copying requires the model to retrieve information from an earlier occurrence of the same text, making it a useful probe for studying how information is organized and accessed internally. Following the use of repeated sequences to study induction heads (Olsson et al., 2022), we inspect Byte-1B with the prompt

Your task is copy the string: X now copy it: X

Both occurrences of XX are supplied in a single teacher-forced causal forward pass. The string contains ten six-word English phrases; each word has exactly 5 ASCII bytes, allowing word boundaries to align across examples. For example, one phrase is "quiet birds cross ocean waves daily". The original and space-free variants contain 35 and 30 bytes, respectively.

E.2 Frozen Layer Intervention

Local span construction.

The frozen layer intervention introduces a compressed global stage over local representations while preserving the original byte-resolution computation before and after the selected layers. Inspired by the local–global–local organization of BLT and H-Net (Pagnoni et al., 2025; Hwang et al., 2026), we identify local spans in the prompts of the 28-layer Byte-1B and Subword-1B models using a matched 200M model from the corresponding family. For a prompt token TiT_{i}, the smaller model with parameters θ\theta computes the token loss

ℒCE​(Ti∣𝐓<i;θ)=−ln⁡pθ​(Ti∣𝐓<i).\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(T_{i}\mid\mathbf{T}_{<i};\theta)=-\ln p_{\theta}(T_{i}\mid\mathbf{T}_{<i}). (19)

Tokens with high loss mark patch boundaries, grouping predictable continuations into local spans.

For text-only tasks with TT prompt tokens, we target ⌈T/4⌉\lceil T/4\rceil patches, corresponding to approximately 4×4\times compression of the text sequence. The first token always starts a patch, and we select the highest loss threshold that yields the target number of patch starts, retaining all ties.

For vision–language tasks with TT non-image prompt tokens and VV image tokens, we apply the same 4×4\times target ratio only to the text portion, giving a target of V+⌈T/4⌉V+\lceil T/4\rceil patches. Each image token is kept as a singleton patch, while text patch boundaries are selected using the same loss threshold procedure. In both settings, prompt patches remain fixed during generation, and each newly generated token is appended as a singleton patch.

Compressed global stage.

Let G=[a,b]G=[a,b] denote the selected layer interval. Before layer aa, the model operates at the original resolution and produces hidden states hih_{i}. For a local span PjP_{j}, we construct a pooled representation

zj=1|Pj|​∑i∈Pjhi.z_{j}=\frac{1}{|P_{j}|}\sum_{i\in P_{j}}h_{i}. (20)

The original layers in GG then operate on the shorter sequence of local representations. After processing, the global updates are mapped back to the original resolution through a residual reconstruction:

h^i=hi+Δj⁡(i),j⁡(i)=max⁡{j:ej≤i}.\hat{h}_{i}=h_{i}+\Delta_{j(i)},\qquad j(i)=\max\{j:e_{j}\leq i\}. (21)

Here, eje_{j} is the final position of span PjP_{j}, and Δj\Delta_{j} is its representation update after the global stage. Tokens before the first completed span keep their original states.

This preserves the original byte-level states while requiring the selected layers to process only local aggregated representations.

F.2 Experimental settings for BPB distribution analysis

We compare models on a 2 MiB subset of the evaluation dataset in Appendix D.1. Subword models are evaluated with sequences of up to 4,096 tokens. Figure 11 shows the full BPB distributions.

H-Net target filtering.

H-Net’s highest BPB values concentrate on TAB (0x09), LF (0x0A), CR (0x0D), { (0x7B), and } (0x7D). H-Net were trained on FineWeb-Edu, a filtered subset of FineWeb. FineWeb’s C4 filter rejects an entire document when a surviving line contains {, also removing any paired } in that document. It drops empty lines and joins retained lines with a single LF, while text extraction collapses whitespace such as TAB and CR. These preprocessing choices may explain the extreme BPB values through reduced training exposure to braces, TAB, CR, and repeated line breaks.

To limit the influence of these formatting differences on the distribution comparison, we exclude the five target characters from H-Net’s distribution statistics while retaining them in the context. H-Net thus retains 98.5% of the full evaluation set.

Finite-range density fits.

To identify the BPB ranges where each density law holds, we use the local power-law exponent and exponential decay scale shown in Figure 12:

αlocal​(x)=d​ln⁡fX​(x)d​ln⁡x,βlocal​(x)=−[d​ln⁡fX​(x)d​x]−1.\alpha_{\rm local}(x)=\frac{d\ln f_{X}(x)}{d\ln x},\qquad\beta_{\rm local}(x)=-\left[\frac{d\ln f_{X}(x)}{dx}\right]^{-1}. (23)

F.3 BPB aggregation ablations

We test the sensitivity of BPB aggregation to tokenizer choice using Byte-1B and BLT-1B. For each model, we average BPB over complete spans defined by the Subword, Qwen3, and Qwen3.5 tokenizers and assign the span mean to each constituent byte. The aggregated distributions are similar across the three tokenizers (Figure 13).

Uniform four-byte grouping.

To test whether average span length alone explains the aggregated distribution, we also use non-overlapping four-byte groups, close to Subword’s average token length in bytes. For both byte models, uniform grouping reduces variation but leaves more near-zero mass and less far-tail mass than tokenizer grouping (Figure 13). These differences highlight the role of tokenizer boundaries in shaping the aggregated BPB distribution.

Tokenizers share most boundaries.

On the evaluation dataset, we find high pairwise boundary Jaccard similarity among the Subword, Llama, Qwen3, and Qwen3.5 tokenizers (Figure 14). These similar boundaries group largely the same bytes together, helping explain the consistency of BPB aggregation across tokenizers.

Appendix G Draft Acceptance and Accepted Text

G.1 Models and evaluation settings

The 200M, 16-layer drafts and the 1B targets come from the main model suite, with the dense configurations in Table 5 and training settings in Appendix B. The 50M drafts use 8-layer models from the IsoFLOPs sweep.

We evaluate documents from the validation dataset in Appendix D.1 within each family’s native context window, 8,192 byte tokens or 2,048 subword tokens, respectively.

G.2 Oracle simulation and acceptance metrics

To isolate draft–target agreement from the strategy used to construct draft candidates, we use an oracle simulation on the given evaluation text. It directly measures consecutive agreements, setting aside choices such as draft-tree expansion, pruning, and stopping heuristics.

Both models condition on the preceding tokens of this text at each scored token (teacher forcing). A draft token is counted as accepted when the two models select the same token, including when it differs from the reference token. The acceptance rate is the fraction of scored tokens accepted. The following step always uses the reference continuation as context. Each verification step ends at the first rejection or document boundary and counts as one simulated target forward pass, with no proposal-length cap.

The mean accepted draft length is the number of accepted draft tokens per simulated target forward pass. To compare text coverage across granularities, we also report accepted bytes per forward, summing the decoded byte lengths of the accepted draft tokens. Both averages include verification steps with no accepted tokens. Special tokens contribute no bytes; correction and bonus outputs are excluded.

Related work uses similar diagnostics of draft–target agreement. Mamou et al. (2024) let the draft continue until the first rejection, identifying the maximum accepted draft length at each iteration without choosing a fixed lookahead or a stopping heuristic. Their oracle follows generated histories, whereas ours measures agreement on the given evaluation text.

EvoESAP (Liu et al., 2026) likewise evaluates acceptance on fixed reference prefixes using teacher forcing. It averages the expected single-token acceptance computed from the overlap between draft and target next-token distributions. Our diagnostic measures consecutive agreements and their byte coverage.

Figure 15 shows high acceptance rates in the lowest-BPB intervals for both families. A much larger share of Byte tokens lies in these intervals, and most of them are accepted. Together with the longer byte acceptance lengths in Table 3, this supports using small drafts to supply many low-BPB byte continuations for joint target verification.

Implications for speculative decoding.

The drafting experiment provides a proof of concept for computation allocation at inference. Longer byte agreement runs indicate that small drafts can match their targets across many consecutive byte tokens in reference text. These runs provide a teacher-forced diagnostic of drafting opportunities. Generated histories may differ from the reference text, so these lengths do not provide a general upper bound on accepted draft length during generation. In speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023), accepted tokens become part of the subsequent context, and each round includes correction or bonus outputs. Establishing practical speedups therefore requires decoding along generated histories with finite proposals and measuring the costs of drafting and target verification.
